newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Farmers study flexible cereals direct aid payments.
newsitem.headline: Farmers study flexible cereals direct aid payments.

text.p: European farmers and farm cooperative groups, COPA/COGECA, are considering variable direct aid payments to cereals farmers, agriculture industry sources said on Thursday.
Direct payments would be lowered or raised according to prevailing market prices enabling substantial budgetary savings when EU and world prices were strong.
Farmers are also studying partly decoupling direct cereals aid payments from production to help prepare for the next round of World Trade Organisation negotiations, the sources added.
Further reforms, following those agreed in 1992, are deemed necessary if the WTO talks result in additional cuts in domestic and export subsidies as well as a further opening of markets.
EU expansion to include eastern and central European countries with major agricultural potential is seen adding extra pressure for reforms.
Direct payments were introduced, as part of reforms agreed in 1992, to compensate farmers for losses caused by cuts in intervention prices and by compulsory set-aside.
Some 18 billion ecus or 40 percent of the EU agriculture budget goes to cereals farmers, with the largest 10 percent receiving most of the subsidies.
The massive payments have become increasingly hard to justify after market prices soared above intervention levels and set-aside limits were substantially reduced.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler last month told farm ministers that cereals farmers were over-compensated and has called for a 1.4 billion ecus cut in payments to help fund aid for beef farmers hit by the mad cow crisis.
Fischler, who has warned that grain mountains will reappear early next century if nothing is changed, is due to present reform proposals later this year.
Agriculture sources said that farmers must continue to be able to sell surplus grain into public intervention stores at a guaranteed price.
They pointed out that the U.S. in its new "Freedom to Farm Act" also retained a safety net for farmers in its marketing loans.
In addition to intervention, EU farmers will demand that compulsory and voluntary set-aside should be maintained to help stabilise prices.
But the EU must avoid set-aside making it the balancing factor on world market and must defend its share of international cereals exports.
Compulsory set-aside can only be enforced if aid paid directly to farmers is linked to production, the sources noted.
Voluntary set-aside can help provide a guaranteed source of supply of raw materials, such as oilseeds, for biofuel and other non-food industrial uses.
Small farmers, notably those represented by Coldiretti in Italy, have strong misgivings about the mooted changes in EU cereals policy, the agricultural sources said.
